children: DuPont de Nemours
, Chemours
and Corteva
agreed to pay $455 million to settle claims involving PFAS contamination in North Carolina, including discharges tied to the Fayetteville Works manufacturing site.

The settlement resolves lawsuits brought by the state and 11 local governments near the plant. It also covers certain statewide claims involving PFAS contamination from other sources, including firefighting foam.

Payments will be made over 15 years, beginning within 30 days of the agreement’s execution. The companies estimated the payments have a combined net present value of about $355 million, reflecting that money paid years from now is worth less than money paid today.

For investors, the agreement removes a significant piece of long-running PFAS litigation at a manageable near-term cash cost, though it does not eliminate the companies’ broader environmental exposure. DuPont’s
pre-tax share has a present value of about $126 million, with 44%, or roughly $55 million, to be reimbursed by Qnity Electronics. That leaves DuPont
with an effective share of about $71 million before taxes and other adjustments. DuPont
said its portion is largely covered by existing reserves, reducing the likelihood of a substantial new charge.

The settlement also satisfies future contributions that the companies otherwise would have been required to make to an escrow account established under a 2021 cost-sharing agreement. That includes a contribution scheduled for September 2026.
Still, PFAS remains a continuing legal risk. DuPont’s

announcement specifically cited pending or potential personal-injury cases, natural-resource damage claims, remediation obligations and changing environmental regulations among the liabilities that could produce additional costs.
Fayetteville Works claims addressed

The settlement covers historical PFAS and other discharges from Fayetteville Works, a chemical manufacturing complex near Fayetteville, North Carolina. Chemicals associated with the site entered the Cape Fear River watershed, which supplies drinking water to communities downstream, including the Wilmington area.

North Carolina regulators, local governments and residents have spent years pursuing treatment, cleanup and compensation related to the contamination. A 2019 consent order previously required Chemours
to reduce emissions, investigate contamination and provide treatment systems for qualifying water supplies near the facility.

The 11 local entities participating in the new settlement are Bladen, Brunswick, Columbus, Cumberland, New Hanover, Robeson and Sampson counties, along with Wrightsville Beach, Lumberton, Bald Head Island and the Lower Cape Fear Water and Sewer Authority.
Those entities had been excluded from a nationwide public-water-system settlement approved in 2024.

Of the $455 million total, $18 million is attributed to contamination allegations not connected to Fayetteville Works. No more than $14.4 million of that amount relates to aqueous film-forming foam, commonly called AFFF. The foam has been widely used to extinguish fuel fires at airports, military bases and industrial sites.
The agreement remains subject to the dismissal of the covered lawsuits.
Why PFAS are called 'forever chemicals'

PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a large family of synthetic chemicals developed for their resistance to heat, grease, stains and water. They have been used in products ranging from nonstick cookware and water-resistant clothing to industrial processes and firefighting foam.
Their unusually strong chemical bonds allow many PFAS compounds to persist for years in water, soil and the human body, earning them the nickname “forever chemicals.”

Exposure to certain PFAS has been associated with increased cholesterol, reduced immune response, developmental effects and greater risk of some cancers, although the risks vary by chemical, dose and duration of exposure. Federal regulators have imposed drinking-water limits on two extensively studied compounds, PFOA and PFOS, while the regulatory treatment of several other PFAS has continued to evolve. The Environmental Protection Agency provides an overview of PFAS and their potential health effects.

PFAS liabilities have become a multibillion-dollar issue for chemical manufacturers because the compounds are widespread and costly to remove from drinking water. The new North Carolina agreement helps define one portion of that exposure for DuPont
, Chemours
and Corteva
, but it doesn't close the book on future PFAS claims.
